definition: Disperse means to scatter in different directions, or to cause a crowd or group to break up and spread out.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word disperse. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know disperse should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: By noon the storm clouds had begun to disperse, leaving patches of clear blue sky.
Spread simply means to cover more area, while disperse means the group actually breaks apart into separate pieces moving different ways.
Disperse is calmer than flee, which adds panic and urgent escape to the scattering.

Scatter is the quick, everyday word for people or things darting off in all directions - marbles scatter, pigeons scatter, startled cats scatter. Disperse is its formal counterpart, the word officials use when a crowd is made to break up. A flock of pigeons scatters; a demonstration is dispersed.

To diffuse is to spread thinly through a surrounding medium, the way a scent diffuses through a room or an idea diffuses through a culture. To disperse is to break a cluster apart into pieces that travel separate ways. Perfume diffuses into the air; a crowd disperses into the streets.

To disband is to dissolve a group as an organization - the committee or the band formally ceases to exist, wherever its members happen to be standing. To disperse is physical: the members move apart in space. A choir can disband by email; it disperses through the parking lot after rehearsal.

Disperse means to scatter in different directions, or to cause a crowd or group to break up and spread out.
A single gust of wind hit the dandelion, and hundreds of seeds dispersed across the meadow.
Within a minute they had drifted so far apart that no two seeds landed anywhere near each other.
The seeds start as one tight cluster and end up scattered in every direction across a wide area, which is precisely the physical spreading-apart that disperse describes.
Disperse describes a group or collection physically breaking apart and moving in different directions, and it is the standard verb for crowds.

Unlike dissipate, which describes something fading away gradually, or dispel, which describes deliberately eliminating a feeling or belief, disperse specifically describes a group or crowd physically scattering in different directions.

The night market in Calle Verde ends the same way every Saturday: at midnight, the string lights blink twice, and the wardens begin their slow sweep.
Their job is to disperse a crowd of nearly two thousand without a single shove.
They do it street by street, closing stalls in sequence so that shoppers drain toward six different exits instead of pressing toward one.

A city report once praised the method for turning what could be a stampede into 'a tide going out.' By half past twelve the square stands empty, though the vendors' association survives intact until the lights blink on again next week.
